q: When extracting a fearful or difficult dog from a kennel using a long slip lead, which mechanical action avoids throwing the lead over the dog's head?
o: Position a bite stick between the door frame and the dog's maxilla
Slide a long sausage treat through the door from the outside to let the dog put her head into the loop
Use a press gate to force the dog's pelvic limbs against the back wall
Apply a flexible snare over the ears while the door is fully open
e: Sliding a treat through the door lets the dog place her own head into the loop, avoiding a stressful over-the-head reach.

q: If a fearful shelter dog is confirmed dog-social, which housing modification is recommended, and what is its main constraint?
o: Group housing in groups of 6 or more, supervised 24/7
Co-kenneling with a more outgoing companion; feed separately to prevent food guarding
Offsite foster only on fixed cycles
Placement next to a predatory species ward with visual blocks
e: Co-kenneling a dog-social fearful dog with an outgoing companion can change her emotional state; feed separately to avoid resource guarding.

q: When a fearful dog needs two handlers with separate slip leads, how should a control pole be used if introduced?
o: As the main tool to direct and lead the dog forward
Only at the time of a dangerous event, while the leashes remain the main tools to direct and lead
Wrapped in a towel to simulate a touch gradient
Applied to the lower lumbar spine for a low centre of gravity
e: The leashes do the directing; the control pole is reserved for the moment of a dangerous event only.

q: Walking a dog down a kennel pod with dogs on both sides, how should the handler position the pair?
o: Dog on a short leash on the right flank, facing the kennels
Maintain the greatest distance possible by keeping the dog in the centre of the aisle
Walk fast while spraying bitter spray into the air
Force the dog to walk backwards with direct eye contact
e: Centring the dog and maximising distance from both rows reduces arousal and bite risk.

q: If a walked dog must face kenneled dogs in a narrow pod, what defensive measure does the handler take?
o: Execute a wheelbarrow technique to speed up
Stand farthest from the kenneled dogs to prevent a redirected bite to the handler
Pick up the drag leash and pull the dog toward the ceiling
Place a vision-blocking device over the handler's own eyes
e: Standing farthest from the kenneled dogs positions the handler away from the likely redirected bite.

q: When initiating contact with a shy or unknown dog, what is the correct orientation and progression?
o: Approach head-on, crouch, and reach over the head to assert control
Turn sideways, crouch if safe, gently toss high-value treats, avoid sudden moves and direct eye contact
Stand fully upright, hands at shoulder height, and talk loudly
Use a syringe pole to inject before any contact
e: A sideways, low, non-confrontational approach with tossed treats lets the dog choose to engage.

q: Once a shy dog solicits contact (leaning or pawing), where should the handler pet?
o: Directly over the top of the head and muzzle
Gently on the side of the shoulder or neck, avoiding reaching over the head
On the hindquarters near the tail base
On the ventral abdomen after rolling the dog over
e: Avoid reaching over the head of a shy dog; pet the side of the shoulder or neck.

q: The touch gradient requires which physical mechanic during an examination?
o: Lifting and lowering the hand on and off the dog to test startle
Moving straight to a pinch or injection with no initial light contact
Touching lightly first and escalating intensity gradually (pet, tap, pinch, inject) while keeping at least one hand in constant contact
Approaching strictly from behind on a taut, short leash
e: The touch gradient (Fear Free) escalates intensity gradually with constant one-hand contact, approaching from the side.

q: How should the team approach an aggressive or fearful dog for a medical procedure?
o: Head-on, reaching over the cranium
From behind, with a snare around the caudal abdomen
From the side, rather than behind or head-on
By lifting straight onto a high table to remove traction
e: Side approach is least threatening and safest for a fearful or aggressive dog.

q: For highly aroused, mouthy, adolescent dogs, which intervention is specifically highlighted to reduce kennel arousal?
o: Long-term containment with zero human contact for 14 days
Standardised doll testing every morning
Sending them to foster care, even for a single night
Mandatory isolation with twice-daily catch-pole conditioning
e: Short foster stays, even one night, help dissipate arousal in mouthy adolescent dogs. (Note: option D was added to complete this item to four options; replace if you prefer.)

q: To keep leverage and balance with a panicking or aggressive dog, where should the hands be?
o: At shoulder height, fully extended away from the body
Low, around belly-button height, and close to the body
Inside the pockets of loose clothing
On the handler's hips to widen the stance
e: Low hands near belly-button height keep a low centre of gravity so the handler is not pulled over. This is a practical heuristic, not a measured constant.

q: Walking a dog known for redirected aggression, which equipment and leash adjustment are used?
o: A flat collar held with a bent elbow near the face
A head halter, a muzzle, or both, while straightening the leash arm to hold the dog away
A flexible snare and a towel wrap around the chest
A chain leash held at shoulder height with crossed hands
e: Head halter and/or muzzle plus a straight leash arm holds a known redirector away from the handler.

q: Which list gives the four actions a handler must NEVER perform when breaking up a dog fight?
o: Use an air horn, deploy a pig board, toss a blanket, scruff the dog
Grab their collars, punch, kick, or pry their mouths apart
Pick up drag leashes, use citronella, blow a whistle, use a break stick
Push objects between them, call for help, use compressed air, turn off lights
e: The four nevers: do not grab collars, punch, kick, or pry mouths apart.

q: During a two-dog fight with non-combatant dogs present, what should secondary handlers do?
o: Deploy break sticks on the non-combatants
Quickly remove the non-combatant dogs to safety, or clip them to the fence with a carabiner
Wheelbarrow all dogs at once
Spray all non-combatants in the eyes with bitter spray
e: Rapidly secure non-combatant dogs (move them to safety or carabiner to the fence) before managing the combatants.

q: What are the inventory and device-check requirements for shelter fight kits?
o: Every 6 months; sprays checked by shaking once
At least every 2 months; sprays checked like a fire extinguisher to confirm they are pressurised and full
Only after a deep gripping fight
Daily, at the end of each lighting cycle
e: Inventory at least every 2 months and verify spray pressure as you would a fire extinguisher; check control poles at the same time.

q: What is the precise sequence for using a break stick on a gripping fight?
o: Grab the tail, insert between molars, pull back with a jerk
Grab the collar at the base of the skull, work the stick parallel to the jaw behind the canine teeth (about 1 inch (2.5 cm) in), and twist the handle
Position the stick perpendicular to the maxilla, slide down the esophagus, push forward
Scruff the flank, slide under the tongue, and lift the dog up
e: Control the head at the base of the skull, insert about 1 inch (2.5 cm) behind the canines parallel to the jaw, then twist to break the grip.

q: Under which conditions is the usual time to gather fight tools overridden, forcing immediate hands-on intervention?
o: Slash-and-dash fights over 15 minutes
Two equal-size aroused adolescents
Large versus small dogs, a blocked airway, or blocked blood flow (tight neck grip with the victim losing consciousness)
A fight during a scheduled scan sample
e: Large versus small, blocked airway, or blocked blood flow are emergencies that remove the usual time buffer.

q: Why is picking up each dog's drag leash and walking apart contraindicated in a gripping fight?
o: It costs the handler their centre of gravity
It triggers redirected aggression onto non-combatants
It does not work on a gripping fight and can increase tissue damage
It invalidates later sedation
e: Opposing pulls on a gripping fight tear tissue and do not separate the dogs.

q: If an off-leash dog grips clothing or a body part and shakes her head, what should the handler do?
o: Push the dog away and pry the jaws with bare fingers
Grab the collar, scruff, or sides of the head to minimise head movement
Immediately curl up and play dead
Swing the dog by its tail
e: Controlling the head (collar, scruff, or sides of the head) limits the damaging shake.

q: The 'feeding the bite' technique relies on which mechanical action to force a release?
o: Pulling the victim backward suddenly
Pushing the biting dog forward into the victim, causing recoil and release
Spraying vinegar into the handler's own sleeves
Rotating a break stick against the belly button
e: Pushing the dog forward into the victim triggers a recoil-and-release reflex (do not pull the victim away).

q: If a dangerous dog pulls a handler to the ground, what is the safest posture?
o: Stand up, scruff the dog, and wheelbarrow it
Curl into a ball, play dead, and cover the neck with the hands
Lie flat on the back, extend the limbs, and scream
Grab a control pole and kink the noose under the body
e: Curling into a ball and covering the neck protects vital structures when downed.

q: Which statement correctly identifies an absolute restriction for control poles?
o: Appropriate for routine use on all incoming small dogs and cats
Never used on a small dog or cat, as severe injury or death may result
Stored by hanging directly by the wire noose to keep tension
Designed mainly to lift large dogs onto tables
e: Control poles are never appropriate for cats or small dogs and are not for routine use, lifting, pushing, or pulling. This aligns with ASV guidance to minimise fear, anxiety and stress and avoid forceful handling.

q: What is the correct way to store a control pole to prevent operational failure?
o: Prop the noose end on the ground by the cleaning charts
Hang it by the wire noose from a high wall to let it stretch
Never hang it by the wire noose or prop the noose on the ground (this kinks the line); hang it by attachments to the pole handle
Lock it inside the fight-kit box under the slip leads
e: Hanging by the noose or propping it on the ground kinks the line; hang by the handle attachments and check regularly.

q: When using an air horn or compressed air to disrupt a fight, what precaution applies?
o: Emit the sound inside the victim's ear canal
Use it as a first resort before checking for drag leashes
Emit compressed air fairly close to the head, but not so close the dog can redirect onto the handler
Hold the air horn at shoulder height facing away
e: Keep compressed air close enough to be effective but not so close the dog can redirect a bite onto the handler.

q: What criteria define when forceful handling (scruffing cats, pinning dogs) is acceptable?
o: When a trainer is unavailable for a scheduled intake exam
Only in extraordinary circumstances, when a human or animal is in immediate danger and other options, sedation, or delays are not possible
Whenever an animal refuses treats during a 15-minute session
To speed operations and reduce length of stay
e: Forceful handling is an emergency last resort only, consistent with ASV guidance against routine forceful restraint.

q: Which housing or handling feature must be preserved to reduce stress for an incoming cat?
o: The cat maintains a sense of control and perceives that escape or hiding is possible
Constant visual contact with predatory canine species
Maximum restraint with a squeeze cage for 48 hours
Repeatedly lifting the hand on and off during care
e: Cats cope better when they retain control and the option to hide, consistent with ASV welfare guidance.

q: What is the correct sequence of the finger-nose technique for socialised cats?
o: Extend a clenched fist rapidly toward the maxilla, then withdraw
Slowly advance an outstretched index finger, hold it in front of the face, let the cat initiate by rubbing, then apply steady pressure to the sides of the face and neck
Slide a finger through a den port to touch the caudal flank
Place a treat on the fingertip and force it into the mouth
e: Advance an outstretched finger, let the cat rub to initiate, then use calm steady pressure on the face, chin, or neck.

q: What was verified about petting sessions for shelter dog stress?
o: Only an intimately familiar owner can change cortisol
About 15 minutes of petting decreased signs of stress even when the volunteer was unfamiliar to the dog
Petting must be on the ventral abdomen with a touch-gradient pinch
Petting is the only effective method; play and passive presence do nothing
e: Roughly 15 minutes of petting reduced stress signs even from an unfamiliar volunteer; play and passive human presence also lower cortisol.

q: For severe leash-grabbing on walks, which is a recommended defensive method?
o: Pull the leash up with both hands until the forelimbs leave the ground
Use a chain leash or cover the lead with PVC pipe, or spray a bad-tasting substance (vinegar or bitter spray) on the lead
Apply a control pole to the base of the skull before leaving the kennel
Use physical force to set handling boundaries
e: PVC-covered or chain leads and a bitter-tasting spray make the lead unrewarding to grab; offering a toy to carry also helps.

q: When returning a dog that wants to stay with people and avoids the kennel, what sequence is used?
o: Drag the dog in with a straight arm and latch the door
Push the hindquarters with a control pole from outside
Toss treats into the corner, or give a food-stuffed toy if resources allow, recognising that high-value food may still not be enough
Stop all walks and switch to passive presence only
e: Toss treats into the corner and offer a food-stuffed toy, while accepting that food alone may not always overcome the dog's preference for people.
